rawInput.complaint:
A 55-year-old man presented with lower urinary tract symptoms characterized by hesitancy, poor urinary stream, and urgency. He denied flank pain, colicky pain, haematuria, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable, and he had no prior genitourinary disease. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs, and a physical examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a serum prostate-specific antigen level of 5.1 ng/ml and a serum creatinine concentration of 86 μmol/l. Urine microscopy demonstrated no haematuria or atypical cells. Transrectal ultrasound–guided prostate biopsies revealed benign prostatic hyperplasia.

An abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate his lower urinary tract symptoms incidentally revealed an exophytic lesion in the right kidney measuring approximately 3.0 × 3.2 × 4.2 cm. The lesion was homogeneous and hypoechoic with a well-defined margin, located at the lateral border of the ventral mid-zone of the kidney. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed a soft-tissue mass in the same location, measuring up to 2.17 cm in maximum diameter, with a small area of calcification; the lesion was exophytic and situated away from the renal hilum.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The patient’s presenting complaint is lower urinary tract symptoms (hesitancy, poor stream, urgency), but the key diagnostic issue in this case is the incidentally discovered right renal mass found during evaluation of those symptoms. His own urinary symptoms are explained by the prostate workup: PSA 5.1 ng/ml with transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsies showing benign prostatic hyperplasia. Therefore, the renal lesion must be assessed as a separate incidental finding.

Salient positive findings for the renal lesion are: a right-sided exophytic renal mass, homogeneous and hypoechoic on ultrasound, well circumscribed, located at the lateral border of the ventral mid-zone, and away from the renal hilum. CT confirmed a small soft-tissue renal mass with a small area of calcification. The lesion appears solid rather than a simple cyst. The patient is 55 years old, which is within the age range where incidental renal neoplasms become more common.

Pertinent negatives are important. He had no flank pain, colicky pain, haematuria, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms; urine microscopy showed no haematuria or atypical cells; creatinine was normal at 86 μmol/l; examination was normal; and there is no prior genitourinary disease. These negatives do not exclude renal malignancy, because many small renal tumors are asymptomatic and incidentally detected, but they make infection, obstructing stone disease, and advanced invasive urothelial processes less likely.

The main differential for a small incidental solid renal mass includes renal cell carcinoma, angiomyolipoma, oncocytoma, and less commonly other benign mesenchymal tumors such as renal leiomyoma. Renal cell carcinoma is the default and most important consideration because a solid enhancing renal mass with calcification in a 55-year-old man is malignant until proven otherwise. Calcification within a renal mass particularly supports RCC over many benign lesions. The exophytic peripheral location is also compatible with RCC.

Angiomyolipoma is less convincing because the imaging description does not mention macroscopic fat, which is the classic CT feature. A homogeneous hypoechoic soft-tissue lesion without fat is not typical for classic AML.

Oncocytoma is plausible because it can present as a well-circumscribed incidental renal mass, but the case does not describe a central stellate scar, and imaging generally cannot reliably distinguish oncocytoma from RCC. Calcification is less characteristic.

Renal leiomyoma is also a consideration because these tumors are often peripheral, well circumscribed, exophytic, and asymptomatic, and may be discovered incidentally. The homogeneous appearance and location away from the hilum fit that pattern. However, renal leiomyoma is rare, and preoperative imaging usually cannot confidently distinguish it from RCC. Given only the clinical and imaging data provided, the most likely working diagnosis remains RCC rather than a rare benign mesenchymal tumor.

Narrowing to a single diagnosis: the lesion is a small, solid, exophytic renal cortical mass with calcification in a middle-aged man, incidentally found and otherwise asymptomatic. Among candidate diagnoses, renal cell carcinoma best fits the available evidence and is the most likely diagnosis clinically, even though some benign entities remain possible on imaging alone.

differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Incidental small solid exophytic renal mass on ultrasound/CT in a 55-year-old man, with soft-tissue density and a small area of calcification; asymptomatic presentation does not exclude RCC.
Well-defined, homogeneous, peripheral exophytic lesion away from the renal hilum is compatible with this rare benign smooth-muscle tumor, but it is uncommon and difficult to diagnose preoperatively.
Can present as a well-circumscribed incidental renal mass, but imaging features given are nonspecific and calcification is less characteristic.
Exophytic renal mass is possible, but CT description does not mention macroscopic fat, making classic AML less likely.
